faqs.a: October to December and February to April are the best months, with dry weather for outdoor yoga and clear mountain views. January is cold in the mornings but bright. From June to September monsoon rain moves most classes indoors and hides the mountains, though prices are lower and Pokhara is quieter.

name: Short breaks in Nepal
tagline: 3 to 5 night Nepal trips that fit a long weekend
meta_description: Short breaks in Nepal from India: 3-night Kathmandu from ₹14,000, 4-night Kathmandu and Pokhara, Chitwan safaris and Lumbini weekends by road.
summary: A short break in Nepal works well from most Indian cities: Delhi to Kathmandu is under two hours by air. We plan 3-night Kathmandu breaks from ₹14,000, 4-night Kathmandu–Pokhara trips, 2-night Chitwan safaris from ₹12,000 and Lumbini weekends from the Sonauli border, with transfers and guides arranged.
intro: Three nights is enough to see the Kathmandu Valley properly. Day one covers Swayambhunath and Kathmandu Durbar Square, day two Pashupatinath and Boudhanath, and day three Bhaktapur, with an optional sunrise at Nagarkot. A 3-night package at a 3-star hotel usually costs ₹14,000–25,000 per person, twin sharing, with private transfers and a guide. Add the one-hour Everest mountain flight on any morning for a close look at the high Himalaya, or a helicopter tour if your budget allows. Delhi to Kathmandu takes about 1 hour 40 minutes, so a Friday-to-Monday trip is realistic.

With four or five nights, add Pokhara. The 25-minute flight from Kathmandu saves a 6–8 hour drive, leaving time for boating on Phewa Lake, sunrise at Sarangkot and tandem paragliding. A 4-night Kathmandu–Pokhara trip costs roughly ₹22,000–35,000 per person at 3-star, plus domestic flights. Chitwan suits a separate 2-night break from ₹12,000–20,000, or a stop between Pokhara and Kathmandu. For travellers near the Uttar Pradesh border, Lumbini and Pokhara can be reached by road from Sonauli in a long weekend.

Short breaks need tight logistics. Choose flights that land in Kathmandu by early afternoon, keep the last day light in case of flight delays, and avoid relying on Lukla or Jomsom flights, which are weather-dependent. Kathmandu traffic can turn a 10 km transfer into an hour. October to April is the best window for clear views; Dashain, Tihar and Diwali weeks fill hotels and raise rates, so book early. Indian citizens need no visa, which keeps last-minute trips simple; check current status before you travel.

how_to_choose.title: Pick one or two bases only
how_to_choose.text: On a short trip, every hotel change costs half a day. With three nights, stay in Kathmandu only; with four or five, split your time between Kathmandu and Pokhara or Chitwan. Save the three-centre circuit for six nights or more.

how_to_choose.title: Fly the long legs
how_to_choose.text: The Kathmandu–Pokhara drive takes 6–8 hours, and the road to Chitwan 5–6 hours. On a short break, the 25-minute flights to Pokhara or Bharatpur buy back most of a day. Keep a buffer of a few hours before your international flight home.

how_to_choose.title: Use mornings for mountain views
how_to_choose.text: Mountains are clearest from sunrise to about 10 am, especially from October to March. Schedule the Everest mountain flight, Sarangkot sunrise or Nagarkot views on your first or second morning, so you still have a backup morning if cloud hides the peaks.

how_to_choose.title: Book transfers in advance
how_to_choose.text: Arriving at Tribhuvan International Airport with a pre-booked car and guide waiting saves time and stress, especially on a short trip. Ask us to arrange your pickup and to advise on SIM cards and currency, so you spend your first afternoon sightseeing rather than queueing.

faqs.q: Is 3 days enough for Nepal?
faqs.a: Three days is enough for the Kathmandu Valley: its seven UNESCO-listed monument zones, plus an optional Everest mountain flight or Nagarkot sunrise. It is not enough for Pokhara or Chitwan as well without rushing. For Kathmandu and Pokhara together, plan four or five nights; for a three-centre circuit including Chitwan, six or more.

faqs.q: What is the cost of a 3-night Kathmandu package?
faqs.a: A 3-night Kathmandu package usually costs ₹14,000–25,000 per person at a 3-star hotel, twin sharing, including breakfast, airport transfers and guided sightseeing by private car. Entry fees, lunches and dinners are often extra. At 4- and 5-star hotels, expect roughly ₹25,000–50,000. Flights from India are not included.

faqs.q: Can I visit Nepal for a weekend from Delhi?
faqs.a: Yes. Delhi to Kathmandu is about 1 hour 40 minutes, so a Friday-evening or Saturday-morning flight gives you two full days in the Kathmandu Valley before returning on Monday. Focus on Pashupatinath, Boudhanath, Swayambhunath and Bhaktapur. Book early around long weekends and festival holidays, when fares rise sharply.

faqs.q: Which is better for a short trip, Kathmandu or Pokhara?
faqs.a: For culture and temples, Kathmandu; for relaxation, lake views and adventure activities, Pokhara. On a 3-night trip, base yourself in one only, because the transfer between them takes either a 25-minute flight plus airport time or a 6–8 hour drive. With four nights or more, do both.

faqs.q: Can I see Everest on a short Nepal trip?
faqs.a: Yes, from the air. The Everest mountain flight by plane takes about an hour from Kathmandu at dawn and fits into any city break. An Everest helicopter tour with a landing takes 4–5 hours and costs US$1,100–1,400 per seat. Both depend on the weather, so book them for your first morning and keep a spare.

faqs.q: What is the best short break from Gorakhpur or Lucknow?
faqs.a: Lumbini and Pokhara work best. From Gorakhpur, the Sonauli border is about 95 km, and Lumbini about 30 km beyond. A 3-night trip can cover Lumbini for one night and Pokhara for two, driving about 185 km from the border to Pokhara. From Lucknow, add roughly 270 km and 5 hours by road to reach Gorakhpur.

name: Overland Nepal tours from India
tagline: Drive into Nepal through six main border crossings
meta_description: Overland Nepal tours from India via Sonauli, Raxaul, Rupaidiha, Kakarbhitta, Jogbani and Banbasa, with distances, vehicle permits and documents.
summary: Six main land crossings link India and Nepal: Sonauli–Belahiya, Raxaul–Birgunj, Rupaidiha–Nepalgunj, Jogbani–Biratnagar, Panitanki–Kakarbhitta and Banbasa–Mahendranagar. Indian citizens cross with a passport or Voter ID and no visa. We plan overland tours by car, coach or train-plus-car, including the customs permits needed for Indian cars and motorcycles.
intro: Sonauli–Belahiya, about 95 km from Gorakhpur, is the busiest crossing for travellers. It leads straight to Bhairahawa and Lumbini, about 30 km away, and on to Pokhara (about 185 km, 7–8 hours) or Kathmandu (about 280 km, 8–10 hours). Raxaul–Birgunj, about 200–220 km from Patna, is the main trade crossing and the quickest road into Chitwan (about 130 km, 3–4 hours) and Kathmandu (about 270 km, 7–9 hours via Hetauda). Rupaidiha–Nepalgunj, about 180–190 km from Lucknow, leads to Bardia National Park and Nepalgunj airport, the gateway for Simikot and Kailash.

In the east, Panitanki–Kakarbhitta, about 35 km from Siliguri and New Jalpaiguri, suits travellers from West Bengal, the Northeast and Darjeeling, with the Ilam tea gardens about 3 hours away and flights from nearby Bhadrapur to Kathmandu. Jogbani–Biratnagar, in Bihar's Araria district, leads to Biratnagar airport and Koshi Tappu. In the far west, Banbasa–Mahendranagar, near Tanakpur in Uttarakhand, is the closest crossing to Delhi by road, about 330–350 km, and leads to Shuklaphanta National Park. Third-country nationals can use these crossings but need a Nepal visa.

Indian cars and motorcycles can enter Nepal with a customs permit called bhansar, issued at the border against the registration certificate, driving licence and insurance, with a daily fee. The number of days allowed each year is limited, and hill roads need confident drivers: Nepal's highways are narrow, landslide-prone in the monsoon and slow, often 30–40 km per hour in the hills. Many travellers prefer to leave their car in India and hire a Nepali vehicle with a driver. Vehicle permit rules and fees change, so check current status before you travel.

how_to_choose.title: Pick the crossing nearest your goal
how_to_choose.text: Choose Sonauli for Lumbini, Pokhara and Muktinath; Raxaul for Chitwan and Kathmandu; Rupaidiha for Bardia and Kailash via Simikot; Kakarbhitta or Jogbani for eastern Nepal and Ilam. Banbasa suits travellers from Uttarakhand and western Uttar Pradesh heading for Shuklaphanta and the far west.

how_to_choose.title: Drive yourself or hire locally
how_to_choose.text: Driving your own car gives freedom but means a bhansar permit, steep hill roads and Nepali traffic rules. Hiring a Nepali car and driver at the border avoids permits and local navigation, and often costs less than you expect. Motorcycle groups should plan shorter riding days in the hills.

how_to_choose.title: Arrive at the border early
how_to_choose.text: Cross in the morning so you reach your first night stop before dark, as night driving on Nepal's hill roads is risky. Customs offices for vehicle permits keep office hours and can be slow at busy times. Allow 30–90 minutes for paperwork at Sonauli or Raxaul.

how_to_choose.title: Mix road and air on long routes
how_to_choose.text: Kathmandu is 7–10 hours from most crossings. Many travellers drive in to Lumbini or Chitwan, fly the long leg to Kathmandu from Bhairahawa, Bharatpur, Biratnagar or Nepalgunj in under an hour, then fly home from Kathmandu. It saves a day without losing the overland experience.

faqs.q: Which is the best border crossing from India to Nepal?
faqs.a: For most tourists, Sonauli–Belahiya is best: it is near Gorakhpur's railway station, close to Lumbini and on the direct road to Pokhara. Raxaul–Birgunj is better from Bihar and for Chitwan or Kathmandu. Kakarbhitta suits travellers from West Bengal and Sikkim. Choose the crossing nearest your first stop in Nepal rather than your home city.

faqs.q: Can I take my Indian car to Nepal?
faqs.a: Yes. At the border customs office you get a bhansar permit for your car by showing the registration certificate, driving licence, insurance and ID, and paying a daily fee. The permit states the number of days, which is limited each year. Carry printed copies of everything. Rules and fees change, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How long does it take to drive from Sonauli to Kathmandu?
faqs.a: About 8–10 hours for roughly 280 km via Butwal, Narayangadh and Mugling, often longer in traffic or roadworks. Many travellers break the journey with a night in Lumbini, Chitwan or Pokhara. For speed, fly from Bhairahawa to Kathmandu in about 35 minutes; Gautam Buddha International Airport is a short drive from the border.

faqs.q: Is the India–Nepal border open 24 hours?
faqs.a: Indian and Nepali citizens can usually cross on foot at most hours, but immigration for third-country nationals and customs offices for vehicles keep set hours, and some crossings close to vehicles at night. Security checks increase around elections and festivals. Plan to cross in daylight. Hours change, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Do Indians need any permit to enter Nepal by road?
faqs.a: Indian citizens need no visa or entry permit, only a valid passport or Voter ID card. There is no immigration stamp for Indians at most crossings, though officials may check your ID. If you bring a vehicle, you need a bhansar customs permit. Trekking areas and national parks need separate permits. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What is the distance from Gorakhpur to Pokhara?
faqs.a: About 280 km: 95 km from Gorakhpur to the Sonauli border, taking 2–2.5 hours, then about 185 km from Belahiya to Pokhara via Butwal and the Siddhartha Highway, taking 7–8 hours. Allow a full day with border formalities. Many travellers break the trip with a night in Lumbini or Tansen.

name: Kailash Mansarovar yatra via Nepal
tagline: Kailash and Manasarovar via Kathmandu or Simikot
meta_description: Kailash Mansarovar yatra via Nepal: Kerung overland and Simikot–Hilsa helicopter routes, costs, parikrama difficulty, best months and passport rules.
summary: The Kailash Mansarovar yatra via Nepal runs from May to September by two main routes: overland from Kathmandu through Kerung (12–15 days, ₹1,90,000–2,60,000) or by flight and helicopter via Nepalgunj, Simikot and Hilsa (₹2,60,000–3,60,000). Both include Lake Manasarovar at 4,590 m and the three-day parikrama over Dolma La.
intro: Mount Kailash (6,638 m) in western Tibet is sacred to Hindus, Buddhists, Jains and Bon followers, and Lake Manasarovar at 4,590 m lies at its foot. From Nepal there are two main routes. The overland route drives from Kathmandu to the Kerung (Kyirong) border, then crosses the Tibetan plateau via Saga to Manasarovar, with acclimatisation nights on the way; it takes 12–15 days and costs about ₹1,90,000–2,60,000. The Simikot route flies Kathmandu–Nepalgunj–Simikot, takes a helicopter to Hilsa and drives to Purang (Taklakot); it is shorter on the road and costs about ₹2,60,000–3,60,000.

The parikrama around Kailash is about 52 km over three days, starting at Darchen (about 4,600 m). Day one follows the valley to Dirapuk, facing the north face; day two crosses Dolma La (about 5,630 m), the hardest day; day three is a shorter walk out via Zutulpuk to Darchen. Yaks, ponies and porters can be hired, and some pilgrims walk only the first section or ride part of the way. Altitude is the main challenge: much of the yatra is above 4,500 m, so a full medical check before booking is essential.

Rules for this yatra change often. Chinese authorities issue the group visa and Tibet permits, and since 2020 the rules for Indian passport holders travelling through Nepal have changed several times, including requirements on visas, biometrics and group size. India's Ministry of External Affairs also runs its own Kailash Mansarovar Yatra via Lipulekh and Nathu La. The season runs from May to September, with Saga Dawa in May or June and the month of Shravan popular with Hindu pilgrims. Check current status before you travel, and book early, as permits take several weeks.

how_to_choose.title: Overland or via Simikot
how_to_choose.text: The Kerung overland route is cheaper and acclimatises you gradually, but involves long drives. The Simikot route uses flights and a helicopter, so it suits those short of time, though weather can delay the Nepalgunj–Simikot and Simikot–Hilsa sectors. Both need about the same fitness for the parikrama.

how_to_choose.title: Check your health honestly
how_to_choose.text: The yatra spends days above 4,500 m and crosses about 5,630 m on foot or horseback. Get a full check-up, including heart, blood pressure and lungs, before booking. People with serious heart or lung disease, uncontrolled diabetes or pregnancy should not go. Age and fitness conditions have been set in some years.

how_to_choose.title: Book early for permits
how_to_choose.text: Tibet permits and the group visa need passport details weeks in advance, and the process for Indian passport holders has had extra steps in recent seasons. Book at least two to three months ahead, keep your passport valid for six months beyond travel, and check current status before you travel.

how_to_choose.title: Compare what the price includes
how_to_choose.text: Check whether the quote includes the Chinese visa, Tibet permits, full board with vegetarian meals, oxygen cylinders, yaks or ponies for the parikrama, helicopter sectors and extra nights for weather delays. Cheaper packages often leave several of these out, which makes them cost more in the end.

faqs.q: What is the cost of Kailash Mansarovar yatra via Nepal?
faqs.a: Overland via Kathmandu and Kerung, a 12–15 day yatra usually costs ₹1,90,000–2,60,000 per person, including the Chinese group visa, Tibet permits, transport and meals. Via Nepalgunj, Simikot and Hilsa with helicopter sectors, expect ₹2,60,000–3,60,000. Ponies or porters for the parikrama, extra nights and travel to Kathmandu are usually extra. Prices change each season.

faqs.q: Can Indian passport holders do Kailash yatra via Nepal?
faqs.a: Indian passport holders travelled to Kailash via Nepal for many years, but since 2020 Chinese rules for Indians on these routes have changed several times, including extra visa procedures, biometrics and fees. The Ministry of External Affairs also runs its own yatra via Lipulekh and Nathu La. We confirm the current rules at booking; check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How difficult is the Kailash parikrama?
faqs.a: The 52 km parikrama takes three days and crosses Dolma La at about 5,630 m. Day two is the hardest, with 8–10 hours of walking at high altitude. Fit adults manage it with good acclimatisation, and ponies and porters help those who need it. The main risks are altitude sickness and cold, so medical fitness matters more than strength.

faqs.q: What is the best time for Kailash Mansarovar yatra?
faqs.a: The season runs from May to September. May, June and September have clearer skies and colder nights; July and August bring some rain, flight delays on the Simikot route and landslides on Nepal's roads. The full moon of Shravan and Saga Dawa in May or June are especially popular dates. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Which is better, Kailash via Simikot or via Kerung?
faqs.a: Kerung, the overland route, is cheaper and acclimatises you more gradually over the drive. Simikot, by flight and helicopter, avoids the long drive from Kathmandu to the border and is a few days shorter, but depends on the weather for small planes and helicopters. Older pilgrims often prefer Simikot for comfort, younger groups Kerung for value.

faqs.q: What documents are needed for Kailash yatra?
faqs.a: You need a passport valid for at least six months, passport-size photos, a medical fitness certificate and the details required for the Chinese group visa and Tibet permits, which the operator files. Indian passport holders may need additional steps, such as biometrics at a Chinese visa centre. A Voter ID is not valid for Tibet. Check current status before you travel.

name: Photography tours in Nepal
tagline: Mountains, temples and wildlife in the best light
meta_description: Photography tours in Nepal: Poon Hill, Sarangkot, Kala Patthar, Boudhanath, Bhaktapur and Chitwan, with best seasons, drone rules and gear advice.
summary: Nepal rewards photographers from October to November, when the air after the monsoon is clear, and again in spring for rhododendrons. We plan photography tours around light: sunrise at Poon Hill or Sarangkot, dusk at Boudhanath, Bhaktapur in early morning, Everest from Kala Patthar and Chitwan wildlife from a jeep.
intro: Mountain light in Nepal is best from October to early December, when post-monsoon air is clean and skies stay clear until late morning. Classic viewpoints include Poon Hill (3,210 m) for sunrise on Dhaulagiri and Annapurna South, Sarangkot above Pokhara for Machhapuchhre reflected in Phewa Lake on calm mornings, and Kala Patthar (5,644 m) for sunset on Everest and Nuptse. Gokyo Ri (5,357 m) gives one of the widest views in the Khumbu, across turquoise lakes to Everest and Cho Oyu. Shoot early: cloud usually builds on the peaks by late morning.

The Kathmandu Valley is full of courtyards, rituals and changing light. Boudhanath at dusk, with butter lamps and pilgrims circling the stupa, Pashupatinath's ghats in early morning, Bhaktapur's Pottery Square and Nyatapola temple at first light, and Patan Durbar Square at blue hour are reliable subjects. Festivals add colour: Indra Jatra, Bisket Jatra in Bhaktapur and the oil lamps of Tihar. Ask before photographing people, never photograph cremations closely, and respect no-photo signs inside temples. A 3–4 night Kathmandu photo itinerary with a local guide covers the main locations at the right times.

Further afield, Upper Mustang's eroded cliffs and the walled town of Lo Manthang, Rara Lake (2,990 m) in the far west and Chitwan's rhinos and birds offer very different work. Flying a drone needs permission from Nepal's authorities, with extra approval inside national parks and near heritage sites; flying without it can lead to confiscation. Cold drains batteries fast above 4,000 m, and charging in teahouses costs extra, so carry spares and a power bank. Drone and permit rules change, so check current status before you travel.

how_to_choose.title: Plan around light, not distance
how_to_choose.text: The best images come in the first two hours after sunrise and the last hour before sunset. Choose itineraries that sleep at or near viewpoints, such as Poon Hill, Sarangkot, Nagarkot or Gorak Shep, rather than driving to them in the dark. Midday is for travel and editing.

how_to_choose.title: Pick the season for your subject
how_to_choose.text: October to November gives the clearest mountains, December to February crisp air and snow-dusted peaks, March to April rhododendrons and hazier views, and the monsoon dramatic cloud and green terraces. Wildlife photographers do best in Chitwan and Bardia from February to April, when the grass is short.

how_to_choose.title: Pack for cold and dust
how_to_choose.text: Above 4,000 m, batteries lose charge quickly and electronics suffer in the cold, while dusty trails and jeep roads get into lenses. Bring spare batteries kept warm in an inner pocket, a power bank, lens cloths and a rain cover. A 24–200 mm range covers most landscape and people shots.

how_to_choose.title: Sort drone and camera rules early
how_to_choose.text: Flying a drone in Nepal needs approval, with extra permission in national parks, heritage zones and near airports. Some monasteries and temples ban photography inside or charge camera fees. Ask us early if you plan drone work so we can advise on the process, and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What is the best time for photography in Nepal?
faqs.a: October and November are best for mountain photography, with clear post-monsoon skies and sharp views until late morning. December to February is also excellent for clear air, though colder. March and April bring rhododendron blooms but more haze. The monsoon, June to September, suits moody cloud, green rice terraces and rain-shadow Mustang.

faqs.q: Can I fly a drone in Nepal?
faqs.a: Yes, with permission. Drone flying in Nepal needs approval from the authorities before you fly, and national parks, conservation areas, heritage sites and airport zones need extra approval or ban drones entirely. Customs may hold a drone at the airport if paperwork is missing. Rules change often; check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Where is the best sunrise view of the Himalaya in Nepal?
faqs.a: Poon Hill (3,210 m) is the classic, with Dhaulagiri, Annapurna South and Machhapuchhre in one frame after a 45–60 minute pre-dawn climb from Ghorepani. Sarangkot above Pokhara is reachable by car. Nagarkot near Kathmandu looks across to the Langtang range. In the Khumbu, Kala Patthar and Gokyo Ri are best known for Everest views.

faqs.q: Is it okay to photograph people and temples in Nepal?
faqs.a: Generally yes, with courtesy. Ask before photographing individuals, especially sadhus, monks and women, and expect sadhus at Pashupatinath to ask for a tip. Do not photograph cremations up close, or inside temples where signs forbid it. Some sites, such as monasteries in Mustang, charge camera fees or ban photography indoors.

faqs.q: What camera lenses should I bring to Nepal?
faqs.a: A 24–70 mm or 24–105 mm zoom handles most temple, street and landscape scenes, and a 70–200 mm or 100–400 mm lens is useful for mountain details and wildlife in Chitwan. A wide-angle lens helps in tight courtyards. Bring a light travel tripod for sunrise and blue-hour shots, and keep weight down if you are trekking.

faqs.q: Can I combine a photography tour with a trek?
faqs.a: Yes. Poon Hill in 4–5 days, the Gokyo and Everest Base Camp treks, and the Annapurna Circuit are all good photography treks. Plan extra nights at key viewpoints, such as two nights at Gokyo, and start early each day. A guide who understands photography timing makes a big difference to what you bring home.

name: Festival tours in Nepal
tagline: Dashain, Tihar, Holi and mask dances on the lunar calendar
meta_description: Festival tours in Nepal: Dashain, Tihar, Holi, Indra Jatra, Bisket Jatra, Mani Rimdu and Tiji, with dates by month, crowds and booking advice.
summary: Nepal's festival calendar follows the lunar year, so dates move each season. The biggest are Dashain and Tihar in September–November, Holi in February–March, Maha Shivaratri at Pashupatinath and Bisket Jatra in mid-April. We plan festival tours around confirmed dates, with hotels booked early and guides who explain the rituals.
intro: Dashain, Nepal's longest festival, runs for 15 days in September or October and honours the goddess Durga. Families gather, elders give tika and jamara, and bamboo swings appear in villages; offices close for the main days, so roads are busy and some services pause. Tihar follows in October or November: crows, dogs and cows are honoured on successive days, houses glow with oil lamps for Laxmi Puja, and Bhai Tika closes the festival. It falls at the same time as Diwali in India. Hotels and flights book out early across both festivals.

Kathmandu's street festivals are its liveliest. Indra Jatra in August or September brings masked dancers and the chariot procession of the living goddess Kumari around Kathmandu Durbar Square. Bisket Jatra in Bhaktapur marks the Nepali New Year in mid-April with chariot pulls through the old town. Rato Machhindranath, Patan's long chariot festival, runs over several weeks in spring. Maha Shivaratri draws large numbers of sadhus and pilgrims to Pashupatinath in February or March, and Holi, called Fagu Purnima, is played in the hills one day before the Terai.

Mountain and Buddhist festivals have their own timing. Mani Rimdu at Tengboche Monastery in October or November features masked dances by monks. Tiji in Lo Manthang, Upper Mustang, takes place in May. Buddha Jayanti in April or May is marked at Lumbini, Boudhanath and Swayambhunath, and Losar, the Tibetan and Sherpa New Year, falls in February or March. In the Terai, Chhath along the rivers and Vivah Panchami in Janakpur draw large crowds. Festival dates depend on the lunar calendar and local decisions, so check current status before you travel.

how_to_choose.title: Confirm the exact dates first
how_to_choose.text: Nepal uses the Bikram Sambat and lunar calendars, so festival dates shift by weeks from year to year. Confirm dates before booking flights, and allow a day either side, as some events such as Tiji or Indra Jatra follow astrologers' or monastery decisions.

how_to_choose.title: Choose spectacle or family ritual
how_to_choose.text: Indra Jatra, Bisket Jatra and Mani Rimdu are public spectacles you can watch from squares and courtyards. Dashain and Tihar are mostly family festivals celebrated at home; you will see lamps, swings and markets, but the heart of them happens indoors. A local guide can explain what you are seeing.

how_to_choose.title: Book rooms well ahead
how_to_choose.text: Hotels in Kathmandu's old towns, Pokhara and near Tengboche fill fast at festival time, and prices rise. Book two to three months ahead for Dashain, Tihar and Indra Jatra, and earlier for Mani Rimdu or Tiji, where lodges are few. Domestic flights around Dashain also sell out.

how_to_choose.title: Expect closures and crowds
how_to_choose.text: During the main days of Dashain and Tihar, offices, banks and some shops close and long-distance buses are packed as people head home. Sightseeing still works, but allow extra time and avoid road travel on peak days. Holi can be messy: wear old clothes and protect cameras.

faqs.q: When is Dashain in Nepal?
faqs.a: Dashain falls in late September or October each year, following the lunar calendar, and lasts 15 days. The most important days are Ghatasthapana at the start, Fulpati on the seventh, Maha Asthami and Maha Navami, and Vijaya Dashami on the tenth, when elders give tika. Offices and many businesses close for several days. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is Tihar the same as Diwali?
faqs.a: Tihar is Nepal's festival of lights and falls at the same time as Diwali in India, usually October or November. It lasts five days, honouring crows, dogs, cows and oxen, with Laxmi Puja on the third day and Bhai Tika, when sisters bless brothers, on the fifth. Houses are lit with oil lamps and decorated with coloured rangoli.

faqs.q: Can tourists watch the Kumari at Indra Jatra?
faqs.a: Yes. During Indra Jatra in August or September, the Kumari, Kathmandu's living goddess, is pulled on a chariot through the old city around Kathmandu Durbar Square over several days. Crowds are large, so arrive early and find a spot near the square or on a rooftop cafe. Photography of the procession is allowed; respect instructions from organisers.

faqs.q: What is the best festival to see in Nepal?
faqs.a: For first-time visitors, Indra Jatra in Kathmandu and Bisket Jatra in Bhaktapur offer the most to watch in public. Tihar is beautiful for its lamps and gentle mood. Maha Shivaratri at Pashupatinath is powerful for Hindu pilgrims. Trekkers can time an Everest trip with Mani Rimdu at Tengboche in October or November.

faqs.q: When is Holi celebrated in Nepal?
faqs.a: Holi, called Fagu Purnima, falls on the full moon of Falgun, usually in March. In Kathmandu and the hills it is celebrated one day before the Terai and India, so you can enjoy it in Kathmandu and then in the Terai the next day. Basantapur and Thamel are the busiest spots. Expect water balloons and colours.

faqs.q: How do I see the Tiji festival in Upper Mustang?
faqs.a: Tiji takes place over three days in Lo Manthang, usually in May, with masked dances by monks re-enacting the victory of good over a demon. Reaching it needs an Upper Mustang restricted area permit, a licensed guide, and either a trek of several days or a jeep from Jomsom. Lodges fill quickly. Check current status before you travel.
